title: Translation & Mediation Skills

pts: The CEFR Companion Volume added mediation as a distinct skill area — relaying and explaining meaning between languages or registers.
This reframes translation and interpreting-adjacent skills as legitimate teaching targets, not a discouraged crutch to be avoided.
This directly updates the CEFR framework first introduced in Unit 2.
points.who: The Council of Europe's CEFR Companion Volume, mediation scales

v: Chart paper; CEFR mediation categories on a handout

items: Ask learners to recall the last time they explained something from one language to someone in another language.
Collect examples on the board: who, what, which languages, why.
Introduce the three CEFR categories: mediating a text, mediating concepts, and mediating communication (Council of Europe 2020).
In groups, learners sort their examples into the three categories.
Discuss: which kinds of mediation will you need most in the future?
Learners keep a ‘mediation diary’ for a week and bring examples to class.
Support: provide example situations to sort.
Challenge: learners read an extract of the CEFR mediation scales and identify the level of one of their own examples.

lines: S1: My grandmother got a letter from the bank in English. I told her in Kannada what it said.
S2: I explained a cricket rule in English to my cousin from the US.
S3: In a group project, I explained the Hindi instructions to a friend from Tamil Nadu in English.
T: Which is mediating a text?
Ss: The bank letter.
T: And S3?
S1: Mediating communication. He helped two people understand each other.

blocks.x: This updates the CEFR introduced in Unit 2 with its newer mediation dimension.

body: Purpose: to show the CEFR mediation categories. Content: three panels: a person reading a document and speaking to another (mediating a text); two people drawing an idea together (mediating concepts); a person standing between two others, with speech bubbles in different scripts (mediating communication). Style: clear, inclusive. Board version: three stick-figure scenes with labels.

items: Council of Europe CEFR website (free) for the Companion Volume and mediation scales.

blocks.x: A handwritten chart of the three categories.

pts: Formal translation aims for a complete, faithful rendering of a text; mediation is a broader, more flexible act of conveying meaning for a specific purpose and audience.
Classroom mediation tasks — summarising a text from one language into another, explaining a concept across languages — are more common and more practical than full translation practice.
This distinction matters for setting realistic classroom goals appropriate to language learners rather than trainee translators.

v: An English notice or circular (written for this book); two audience cards

items: Give learners a short English school circular.
Group A translates it fully into a home language.
Group B explains it orally in a home language to an imagined audience (a grandparent who needs only the key information).
Groups compare: what did each include and omit? Which took longer? Which was more useful for the audience?
Conclude that translation aims at complete, faithful rendering; mediation selects and adapts for a purpose and audience.
Reverse the direction: a notice in Hindi or Kannada is mediated into English for a visiting teacher.
Support: highlight the key information in the circular beforehand.
Challenge: learners write a one-paragraph reflection on what was lost and gained in each version.

lines: Parents are requested to note that, owing to the scheduled maintenance of the electrical supply, the school will function from 7.30 a.m. to 11.30 a.m. on Saturday, 14 September. Mid-day meals will be served at 11.00 a.m. Buses will run at the revised timings.

blocks.x: A mediated oral version for a grandparent, reported in English:

lines: On Saturday school is only in the morning, till 11.30. Lunch is at 11. The bus comes earlier.
T: What did the mediator leave out?
S1: The reason. The electricity.
T: Was that a good decision?
S2: Yes. Grandmother doesn’t need it.

body: Purpose: to contrast translation and mediation. Content: one document on the left; an arrow to a full, same-length document labelled ‘translation’; another arrow to a short speech bubble aimed at a listener, labelled ‘mediation’. Style: clean. Board version: a rectangle with two arrows to a rectangle and a bubble.

items: Bhashini (free, Government of India) and Google Translate (free) to compare a machine translation with a human mediation.

blocks.x: A printed circular and oral work in pairs.

pts: Strategic, purposeful L1 use — for mediation tasks, complex concept-checking, or metalinguistic discussion — differs from unstructured reliance on L1 to avoid the target language.
This complicates the traditional communicative-methodology assumption that L1 should be minimised at all costs.
The distinction is purposeful integration versus avoidance-driven default, not simply how much L1 is used.

v: A recorded or remembered lesson; a list of own-language functions

items: Record ten minutes of a lesson (with consent), or recall one in detail.
Note every moment when you or learners used a language other than English.
Classify each moment: purposeful (mediation task, concept check, metalinguistic discussion, emotional support) or avoidance (defaulting to the home language when English was possible).
Discuss with a colleague which purposeful uses to keep and which avoidance patterns to change.
Plan one explicit routine, for example a two-minute home-language concept check after a difficult grammar explanation.
Survey learners anonymously: when does using your home language help you learn English?
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Home-language use 1: I explained ‘present perfect’ in Kannada after two English attempts failed. → purposeful (concept check).
Home-language use 2: Group 3 discussed the speaking task entirely in Hindi. → avoidance (task was within their English level).
Home-language use 3: a learner comforted a classmate in Urdu. → purposeful (emotional support).

blocks.x: The question is not how much of the home language is used but why (Hall and Cook 2012). This complicates the communicative assumption that the home language should be minimized at all costs (Cook 2010).

body: Purpose: to show the key distinction. Content: two paths from the same learner: one labelled ‘purposeful’ leads through a bridge to English; the other labelled ‘avoidance’ loops back to the start. Style: simple, non-judgemental. Board version: two arrows, one straight to a goal and one curving back.

items: A phone’s voice recorder (free) to capture a lesson extract.

blocks.x: A tally sheet with two columns, completed by a peer observer.

body: The CEFR Companion Volume describes the learner as a ‘social agent’ with a plurilingual repertoire, in which languages interact rather than sitting in separate compartments. Mediation scales are written so that they can be used whether one or two languages are involved.

pts: Many real-world English users regularly mediate — summarising an English document for a colleague, explaining a concept across languages informally.
This connects to Unit 2's needs analysis — for many learners, mediation is a genuine, high-frequency real-world need worth direct classroom attention.
Task design here should mirror this real-world mediating function, not artificial translation exercises.

v: Authentic documents (a bus timetable, a medicine leaflet, a job advertisement); role cards

items: Ask learners where they, or adults they know, mediate in real life (Unit 2).
Choose three situations from their answers and prepare an authentic document for each.
In pairs, one learner is the mediator and the other is the audience with a specific need (role card).
The mediator conveys what the audience needs, in the language the audience prefers, then summarizes in English for the teacher.
Pairs swap roles with a different document.
For older learners, use workplace documents: an English safety notice mediated for Kannada-speaking construction workers, or a Hindi customer complaint mediated into an English email to head office.
Support: shorter documents with key information marked.
Challenge: the audience card includes a constraint (the listener is in a hurry; the listener is worried and needs reassurance).

blocks.x: A role card and mediation (written for this book):

lines: Audience card: You are a Telugu-speaking parent. Your child has a fever. You want to know how much of this medicine to give and when.
Mediator’s English summary for the teacher: I told her in Telugu: for a child of her age, half a spoon three times a day after food, and to see the doctor if the fever lasts more than two days.
T: Did you tell her about the ingredients?
S1: No. She didn’t ask, and she doesn’t need it.

blocks.x: Task design mirrors the real mediating function, not an artificial sentence-by-sentence translation exercise.

body: Purpose: to show mediation in real life. Content: four small scenes: a young person reading a leaflet to a parent; an office worker summarizing a meeting in an email; a tour guide between visitors and a shopkeeper; a nurse explaining instructions to a patient. Style: warm, Indian settings. Board version: four boxes with one-word labels.

items: Google Lens (free) to scan a printed document and view a translation, used to check rather than replace the learner’s mediation.

blocks.x: Authentic leaflets, timetables and notices collected from the local area.

pts: Mediation draws on strategic competence (Unit 27) — paraphrase, simplification, cultural explanation — applied specifically across languages.
Explicit strategy teaching (identifying core meaning, choosing what to omit, adapting register for the new audience) makes this skill more accessible.
This connects directly to Unit 27's strategic-competence teaching, extended into a cross-linguistic context.

v: A dense English paragraph (written for this book); strategy cards

items: Introduce four strategies: identify the core meaning; decide what to omit; simplify or explain terms; adapt register for the audience.
Model all four aloud with a short dense text.
In pairs, learners mediate a second text for a specified audience, ticking the strategy cards as they use them.
Listeners give feedback: was anything essential lost? Was the register right?
Learners note which strategy they found hardest and practise it with a third text.
Practise within English: mediate a technical paragraph into plain English for a younger learner.
Support: provide the core meaning; learners focus on register.
Challenge: learners mediate for two different audiences and compare their choices.

blocks.x: A dense paragraph (written for this book):

lines: Participants exhibiting symptoms consistent with dengue, including persistent high fever, severe headache and retro-orbital pain, are advised to seek clinical evaluation without delay and to refrain from self-medication with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Core meaning: if you think you have dengue, see a doctor quickly and don’t take certain painkillers.
Omit: ‘participants’, the formal register.
Explain: ‘retro-orbital pain’ = pain behind the eyes; ‘NSAIDs’ = painkillers like ibuprofen; paracetamol is different.
Adapt: speak simply and directly, in Tamil, to a neighbour.

blocks.x: These strategies draw on strategic competence (Unit 27), applied across languages.

body: Purpose: to name mediation strategies. Content: an open toolbox with four labelled tools: a magnifying glass (core meaning), scissors (omit), a lamp (explain) and a dial (adapt register). Style: friendly, iconographic. Board version: four simple icons with labels.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for printable strategy cards.

blocks.x: Four strategy cards made from scrap paper.

pts: In multilingual classrooms, learners' full linguistic repertoire is a resource for mediation practice, not a problem to be minimised.
This previews Unit 71's translanguaging work — mediation and translanguaging pedagogy share a common underlying philosophy.
Peer mediation tasks between learners sharing an L1 can build this skill in an immediately authentic context.

v: A short English text; a class language map

items: Make a class language map: which languages does each learner speak, read or understand?
Pair learners who share a home language, and learners who share none.
Shared-language pairs: one learner reads an English text and explains it to the partner in the shared language; the partner checks by asking questions.
Mixed pairs: the same task, but the mediation is from difficult English into simpler English.
Discuss what each type of pair found easy or difficult.
In classes where one language dominates, invite learners who speak minority languages to teach the class key words, reversing the usual direction of mediation.
Support: stronger English readers mediate for less confident partners, then swap for a text in the partner’s stronger area.
Challenge: learners mediate the same text for two partners who speak different languages.

lines: A: I explained the science paragraph in Urdu. She understood ‘evaporation’ when I said bhaap banna.
B: Then I asked her in English, ‘So what happens to the water?’ and she answered in English.
T: So the home language opened the door, and then English came through it.

blocks.x: This previews Unit 71: mediation and translanguaging share the idea that learners’ whole repertoire is a resource.

body: Purpose: to show the class’s multilingual repertoire. Content: a map of learners’ names connected by coloured threads, one colour per language (Kannada, Hindi, Urdu, Tamil, Telugu, English), with labels as well as colours. Style: warm, collaborative. Board version: names in a circle joined by lines labelled with language names.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) word cloud of the languages in the class.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn language map on chart paper.

body: Build the language map at the start of the year and keep it on the wall. It helps you plan pairings, reminds learners that their languages are valued, and often reveals languages you did not know were in the room.

pts: Assess whether the core meaning and appropriate register transferred to the new context, not word-for-word linguistic accuracy alone.
The CEFR's mediation scales provide a starting reference point for building task-specific rubrics in this newer skill area.
This connects to Unit 46's rubric-design principles, applied to genuinely newer, less-established assessment territory.

v: CEFR mediation scales; three recorded or written learner mediations

items: Select the relevant CEFR scale, for example ‘Relaying specific information’ or ‘Processing text’ (Council of Europe 2020).
Draft four criteria: core meaning conveyed, relevance to audience need, register and tone, and language control in the target language.
Weight core meaning and audience relevance above word-level accuracy (Unit 46).
Score three mediations with a colleague and agree benchmarks.
Record which criterion caused most disagreement and refine its descriptors.
Where teachers do not share the learner’s home language, assess the English summary the learner gives of what they mediated, or pair with a colleague who does.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Descriptors for ‘core meaning conveyed’ (written for this book):

lines: 4: All information the audience needs is conveyed accurately; nothing essential is omitted.
3: Most essential information conveyed; one minor omission or inaccuracy.
2: Some essential information missing or distorted.
1: The audience could not act on what was conveyed.
A: This learner’s Hindi mediation had grammar errors.
B: But the parent would know exactly what to do. That’s a 4 for meaning and a 2 for language control.

blocks.x: Mediation assessment is newer territory than the four skills, so rubrics need trialling and revision.

body: Purpose: to show assessment of mediation. Content: a suitcase labelled ‘meaning’ carried across a bridge between two language islands; a checklist beside it asks ‘arrived complete? suited to the traveller? right tone?’. Style: clear, metaphorical. Board version: two circles joined by a bridge, with three questions beside it.

items: Google Sheets (free) for comparing rater scores.

blocks.x: Paper rubrics and a class score grid.

pts: Many professional and academic contexts explicitly value mediation ability — briefing colleagues, summarising research, cross-team communication.
This connects to Unit 65's ESP course design, where mediation is often a genuinely core, rather than peripheral, professional skill.
Naming and teaching mediation explicitly gives it the same pedagogical status as the four traditional skills.

v: A short English report (written for this book); a scenario card

items: Present a workplace scenario: a manager needs a two-minute briefing on an English report before a meeting.
Learners read the report and prepare notes for an oral briefing.
In pairs, the manager asks questions; the mediator briefs and responds.
Learners then write the same briefing as a five-line email for a colleague who missed the meeting.
Discuss which professional roles your learners aim for and what mediation those roles involve (Unit 65).
For teacher-trainees, mediate a research summary on reading instruction for a group of parents at a school meeting.
Support: provide a briefing template (purpose, key finding, implication, action).
Challenge: the manager has a different first language, and the briefing must be adapted for them.

blocks.x: A spoken briefing (written for this book):

lines: T: Right, what do I need to know?
S1: The report says the pilot improved reading in 30 schools. The main reason was daily reading time, not the new books.
T: What does it mean for us?
S1: We should protect twenty minutes a day for reading before we spend on materials.
Subject: Reading pilot, key points

The pilot improved reading scores in 30 schools. The report credits daily reading time more than new materials. Recommendation: protect 20 minutes of reading daily before buying new books. Full report attached.

blocks.x: Naming mediation gives it the same pedagogical status as the four traditional skills.

body: Purpose: to show mediation in professional settings. Content: a thick report on a desk, a person condensing it into three bullet points on a card, and a small group around a table listening. Style: clean, professional, Indian office setting. Board version: a large rectangle, an arrow, and a small card with three dots.

items: Microsoft Outlook or Gmail (free) for drafting a model briefing email.

blocks.x: A briefing card written by hand and delivered orally.

body: For one week, ask each learner to record one real moment of mediation in their life, in any language combination. In the following lesson, choose two of these moments and turn them into classroom tasks. Notice how much more engaged learners are when the task is one they have already faced.

dek: Unit 64 of 100: moving meaning between languages is its own distinct competence — increasingly recognised as a legitimate classroom skill, not a discouraged shortcut.

aims.x: For decades, many teachers were trained to see translation as a shortcut to be avoided and the learner’s home language as something to be kept out of the English classroom. Yet much of what English users actually do every day involves moving meaning between languages: explaining an English circular to a parent in Kannada, summarizing a Hindi meeting in an English email, helping a new colleague understand a form. This unit treats that activity, now called mediation in the CEFR, as a skill to be taught and assessed, and shows how it fits multilingual Indian classrooms.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what the CEFR Companion Volume means by mediation and why it was added;
distinguish formal translation from mediation and set realistic classroom goals;
distinguish purposeful own-language use from avoidance of English;
design mediation tasks based on real-world situations your learners face;
teach mediation strategies such as identifying core meaning, simplifying and adapting register;
use learners’ full linguistic repertoire, including peers who share a language, as a resource;
build a task-specific rubric for mediation, drawing on the CEFR scales;
connect mediation to professional and academic needs.

why: Why this matters. Translation was long dismissed in communicative methodology. Current frameworks like the CEFR now recognise mediation as a genuine, teachable fifth skill.

background.x: The original Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe 2001) mentioned mediation briefly, alongside reception, production and interaction, but gave it no descriptor scales. The Companion Volume (Council of Europe 2020) changed this. Drawing on a large development project led by Brian North and Enrica Piccardo (North and Piccardo 2016), it provided illustrative scales for mediating a text (for example, relaying specific information or explaining data), mediating concepts (collaborating to construct meaning), and mediating communication (facilitating across cultures, acting as an intermediary). It also described mediation strategies such as linking to previous knowledge, adapting language, amplifying a dense text and streamlining it. Mediation can happen within one language (explaining a technical English text in plain English) or across languages.

This recognition came after a long reassessment of translation in language teaching. Guy Cook (2010) argued that the rejection of translation in the twentieth century was based more on the needs of commercial, monolingual teaching than on evidence, and that translation can support accuracy, awareness and real-world communication. Graham Hall and Cook (2012) reviewed research on own-language use and concluded that it has important functions in learning, while cautioning that its purpose matters. Philip Kerr (2014) provided a practical resource book of translation and own-language activities. Jim Cummins (2007) challenged the ‘two solitudes’ assumption that languages must be kept strictly separate in bilingual education.

For India, these ideas are not new so much as overdue. Most Indians mediate daily between two, three or more languages, and the three-language formula assumes multilingual schooling. NEP 2020 supports teaching in the home language or mother tongue where possible, bilingual approaches and a strong emphasis on translation and interpretation, and proposes an institute for translation and interpretation (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 describes multilingualism as a resource for learning (NCERT 2023). Government platforms such as Bhashini now offer machine translation among Indian languages, making mediation a live question for learners who will use such tools at work.

Mediation also has limits worth naming. It is not an excuse to abandon English practice, and not every learner in a class shares the same home language. The skill is choosing what to convey, to whom, in which language and register, and for what purpose. Unit 71 develops the related idea of translanguaging in depth; this unit focuses on mediation as a teachable, assessable competence.

items: Mediation task. An oral or written mediation of an authentic document for a specified audience, scored with a meaning-focused rubric.
Strategy commentary. Learners annotate a mediation with the strategies they used and explain one choice to omit or adapt.
Mediation diary. A week’s record of real mediation, classified by CEFR category.
Professional briefing. A spoken briefing and a short written summary of the same English report.
What were you taught about translation and the home language during your own teacher education? Has your view changed?
In your last lesson, which uses of a language other than English were purposeful, and which were avoidance?
What mediation do your learners already do outside school?
How can you assess mediation fairly when you do not speak all your learners’ languages?
How should learners use machine translation tools as mediators, and when should they not?
Which professional roles your learners aim for depend most on mediation?

terms.def: A CEFR category of mediation in which a user passes on the content of a text to someone who cannot access it, for example summarizing an English notice in Kannada for a parent (Council of Europe 2020).
A CEFR category of mediation in which a user facilitates communication between people, for example across cultures or languages, acting as an intermediary (Council of Europe 2020).
A CEFR category of mediation in which a user helps others build or understand new ideas, often through collaborative group work (Council of Europe 2020).

1. In the CEFR, making meaning accessible to others, within or across languages, by relaying texts, explaining concepts or facilitating communication (Council of Europe 2020). 2. In sociocultural theory, the way tools, especially language, shape thinking and learning.
Techniques used when mediating, such as linking to previous knowledge, adapting language, amplifying a dense text or streamlining it (Council of Europe 2020).
The deliberate use of learners’ first or home languages in English lessons, for example for explanation, comparison or mediation, as a resource rather than a failure.
The interconnected set of languages and language knowledge a person has, which they can draw on flexibly when communicating or learning (Council of Europe 2020).

A mediation strategy in which a speaker or writer adjusts the formality, technicality or style of a message for a new audience, for example explaining a formal circular from the school office in simple everyday language for parents.

The CEFR’s view of the language learner as a person acting in society with a plurilingual repertoire, in which languages interact rather than being kept separate (Council of Europe 2020). It underpins the CEFR’s mediation scales.
Conveying the meaning of a text from one language to another. In the classroom it is distinguished from broader mediation and can be a valuable, purposeful activity rather than a shortcut to avoid.
